passage:
Week one: Abhinav walked past the college career fair twice and didn't go in. Everyone inside seemed confident, shaking hands. He told himself he'd go next year.

Week three: At an alumni talk in the seminar hall, a former student named Mridul described working at a small robotics firm. After the talk, Abhinav's palms were sweating, but he walked up. "Sir, how did you get your first internship?" Mridul laughed. "Don't call me sir. Email me your project, I'll look." Abhinav went back to the hostel and wrote the email three times before sending it.

Week seven: Mridul had replied with feedback and the name of a manager at the firm. Abhinav had an interview on Friday. He ironed his shirt the night before, nervous but ready.

qa.q: What kind of firm did Mridul work at?
qa.a: A small robotics firm.

qa.q: What does Abhinav's sweating palms suggest when he approached Mridul?
qa.a: He was nervous and afraid of seeming pushy, but he wanted the connection enough to go up anyway.

qa.q: What small step helped Abhinav most, and why?
qa.a: Emailing his project, because it gave Mridul something concrete to look at and turned a brief chat into a real professional link.

qa.q: How might Mridul see the student who came up after his talk?
qa.a: He likely remembered his own early days and was happy to help a junior who showed real interest and followed up.

grounding: Shows over several weeks a student taking first steps to find a mentor and an internship through networking.

passage: "Abhinav, you're sulking because nobody replied to your applications, right? Sit. Let me tell you how I got my first break. I was twenty and too shy to talk to anyone at college events. My Chemistry professor noticed I always stayed back to clean the lab. One day she asked, "Ira, why do you care so much?" I told her about my idea for testing water in our village. She said, 'Write it up.' I did, badly. She fixed half of it. Then she introduced me to a researcher at a state lab who needed an intern. That researcher became my mentor for ten years. You see? It wasn't the applications. It was one person seeing my work and me being brave enough to follow up. Who has seen your work?"

qa.q: What did Ira's professor notice?
qa.a: That Ira always stayed back to clean the lab.

qa.q: What does Ira think Abhinav is feeling at the start?
qa.a: Ira thinks Abhinav is discouraged and sulking because the applications got no replies.

qa.q: What would Ira advise Abhinav to do next?
qa.a: Find someone who has seen Abhinav's work, share it with them, and follow up bravely, instead of relying only on applications.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel after hearing the elder's story?
qa.a: Abhinav may feel less rejected and more hopeful, seeing that relationships can open doors that cold applications don't.

grounding: An elder tells a young adult how a first mentor and internship came through one relationship and follow-up.

passage: Irfan's cousin Jeevan had set up an informal chat with a senior architect at her firm, 10 a.m. on Thursday, the kind of meeting that could lead to an internship. On Thursday morning, the local train stopped between stations for forty minutes. No signal inside the packed compartment. Irfan's heart raced as the clock ticked past ten. When the train finally moved, he got off at the next stop, found a corner away from the crowd and called Jeevan. Then he emailed the architect directly: a short apology, the reason, and two alternative times. He attached his portfolio, just in case. By evening, the architect replied: "Trains happen. Monday at noon works. Nice portfolio." Irfan let out a breath he felt he'd been holding all day.

qa.q: What time was Irfan's original chat with the architect?
qa.a: At 10 a.m. on Thursday.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling as the clock passed ten?
qa.a: He was anxious and afraid he'd lose the chance and embarrass his cousin, which is why his heart raced.

qa.q: Which choice helped Irfan save the opportunity?
qa.a: Quickly emailing a clear apology with new times and his portfolio, which showed responsibility and kept the conversation going.

qa.q: How might Jeevan feel about the way Irfan handled the delay?
qa.a: She would likely be relieved and proud, since his calm follow-up reflected well on her recommendation.

grounding: Shows a young adult handling an obstacle while trying to secure a mentor connection and possible internship.

passage: The alumni meet in the college auditorium in Delhi was loud, and Divyansh, twenty-one, stood by the snacks table holding a paper cup for twenty minutes. He had printed three copies of his CV, and they were going soft in his bag. Then he saw Deepika, a senior from four batches ahead who now worked at a water-treatment firm he had read about. He walked over before he could stop himself. 'Ma'am, sorry, I read your project on low-cost filters. Could I ask how you got into that field?' She laughed. 'Deepika, please. Not ma'am.' They talked for ten minutes. She told him about a summer internship nobody applied to because it was in a small town. 'Email me tonight. Mention the filters.' He did, at 11:40 pm, after four drafts.

qa.q: How many copies of his CV had Divyansh printed?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: What does Divyansh standing by the snacks table for twenty minutes suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt nervous and shy about approaching people.

qa.q: Which of Divyansh's choices helped the conversation work?
qa.a: Mentioning her actual project showed genuine interest, which made her willing to help.

qa.q: How might Deepika have seen Divyansh's approach?
qa.a: She probably liked that he had read her work and was glad to help a junior who seemed sincere.

grounding: Shows a young adult making a first professional contact that opens an internship lead.

passage:
'Tanvir Mamu, can I ask you something awkward?'
'Those are my favourite.'
Jaya pushed her plate aside. 'You know people at architecture firms. I've applied to eleven internships online. Nothing.'
'And you want me to call someone.'
'No! I mean... I don't know what I want.'
He smiled. 'Here's what I can do. I'll introduce you to one person, my old classmate. Not to get you a job. To have tea and ask questions.'
'What questions?'
'What she wishes she'd known at twenty. What her firm looks for. Then you listen more than you talk.'
'And after?'
'After, you send a short thank-you message. And you don't ask for anything the first time.'
Jaya nodded slowly. 'That's harder than applying online.'
'Yes. It's also how most of us got our first break.'

qa.q: How many internships had Jaya applied to online?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: What does Jaya's 'I don't know what I want' suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She felt awkward about asking for favours and unsure how to use her uncle's connections.

qa.q: What does Mamu's advice teach about early networking?
qa.a: Start with a genuine conversation, listen and say thanks, rather than asking for a job straight away.

qa.q: How might Mamu's classmate see a tea meeting like this?
qa.a: She would likely be happy to share advice with someone who comes to learn rather than to demand a job.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult learning, through family, how to build a first mentoring relationship in her field.

passage: I'm Baljeet. In my second year, I went to a design workshop in Chandigarh and almost didn't speak to anyone. The main speaker was Jasleen, who ran a small studio I admired. At the tea break, my hands were shaking, but I walked up and said, "I liked how you explained colour. Could I show you my sketchbook?" She flipped through it, said, "Your layouts are strong, your lettering needs work," and gave me her email. I wrote to her the next day, thanking her. Two months later, she offered me a summer internship. I still email her when I'm stuck.

qa.q: What did Jasleen say needed work?
qa.a: The lettering.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel walking up to Jasleen at the tea break?
qa.a: Baljeet felt nervous and shaky, but determined not to miss the chance.

qa.q: What small steps helped Baljeet build this connection?
qa.a: Speaking up at the break, showing real work and following up with a thank-you email the next day.

qa.q: How might Jasleen have seen Baljeet's approach?
qa.a: As brave and sincere, which made her willing to offer advice and later an internship.

grounding: Shows a young adult building a first professional connection that leads to a mentor and an internship.

passage:
Internship supervisor's note, Sharmila, June
Harish (20) has been with our NGO for four weeks. He asks good questions and writes down the answers. In week two he asked if he could sit in on the field team's meetings, and he now shadows our programme lead on Tuesdays. He's also reached out to two of our older volunteers for advice about careers in public health research. He's a little shy in large meetings, but one-to-one he's thoughtful. I've offered to write him a reference and introduced him to a researcher I know.

qa.q: How long has Harish been with the NGO?
qa.a: Four weeks.

qa.q: What might Harish feel in large meetings?
qa.a: He probably feels shy and a little anxious, though he's confident one-to-one.

qa.q: Why is Sharmila's introduction a helpful next step?
qa.a: It connects Harish with someone in the exact field he's interested in, building his network.

qa.q: How might the programme lead see Harish shadowing on Tuesdays?
qa.a: As a sign of real interest, and maybe as someone worth mentoring.

grounding: Shows a young adult building professional relationships and seeking mentors during an internship, noted by his supervisor.

passage:
Lalremsiami's diary, Wednesday
Sent ten emails this week asking for architecture internships. Nine no replies. One polite "no". I cried a bit in the hostel bathroom, then felt silly. Tonight Hafsa, the senior from my department, found me in the common room and asked what was wrong. She said, "Cold emails rarely work. Come with me to the alumni meet on Saturday." She's going to introduce me to two people she worked with. I'm terrified of small talk, but I'll prepare three questions about their projects. Hafsa said, "People help people they've met." I really hope she's right.

qa.q: How many internship emails did Lalremsiami send?
qa.a: Ten emails.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami feel after getting no replies?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt discouraged and sad, and then a bit silly for crying.

qa.q: What would you advise Lalremsiami before the alumni meet?
qa.a: Prepare those three questions, listen well and follow up with a short thank-you message afterwards.

qa.q: How might Hafsa see helping a junior student?
qa.a: She seems to see it as natural and kind, perhaps remembering her own start.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning that building personal connections helps secure internships.

passage: The Krishi Vigyan Kendra office in Jalna had a slow ceiling fan and a line of farmers. Lokesh, twenty-one, an agriculture student, waited forty minutes with a folder under his arm. When his turn came, the officer, Sangeeta Patil, looked up. "Yes?" Lokesh's mouth went dry. "Ma'am, I'm in my third year. I want to learn how you run the soil-testing programme. Can I help during my holidays? Unpaid is fine." She raised her eyebrows. "Why us?" "My father's farm lost a crop to wrong fertiliser last year. I want to understand soil properly." She was quiet, then wrote a phone number on a slip. "Come Monday at nine. Wear shoes you can get muddy in." Lokesh walked out, grinning at the sky.

qa.q: How long did Lokesh wait?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling when his mouth went dry?
qa.a: He felt nervous about asking the officer directly.

qa.q: What made Lokesh's approach work?
qa.a: He was direct and polite and gave a real reason for wanting to learn.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta Patil see Lokesh's request?
qa.a: She seemed surprised, then impressed by his sincerity and the reason behind it.

grounding: A young agriculture student in a small town walks in to ask an officer for a learning placement.

passage: At the design meetup in Buenos Aires, Sofia, twenty-two, held a glass of juice and watched people laugh in small circles. She'd come because her professor had said, "Meet people, not just portfolios." Across the room was Layla, a designer whose book covers Sofia had admired for years. Sofia's heart thumped. She almost left. Then she walked over during a pause. "Hi, I'm Sofia. I study design at the university. I love the cover you did with the paper birds." Layla smiled. "Thank you! Are you into book covers?" They talked for fifteen minutes. At the end, Layla handed her a card. "Send me a few of your pieces. I sometimes need an assistant." Sofia floated all the way home.

qa.q: What did Sofia admire in one of Layla's covers?
qa.a: The paper birds.

qa.q: How did Sofia feel before walking over to Layla?
qa.a: She felt very nervous, with a thumping heart, almost leaving.

qa.q: What did Sofia do that made the conversation work?
qa.a: She introduced herself simply and mentioned a specific cover she admired.

qa.q: How might Layla see Sofia's approach?
qa.a: Layla probably found it genuine and flattering, which is why she offered her card.

grounding: A young design student in Argentina overcomes nerves to approach a designer she admires at a meetup.

passage:
At the college career fair, held in the badminton hall, Darshan stood by the architecture firm stalls with a folder of printed drawings, too shy to walk up.
Ritu, from his batch, came over. "You've been standing here for twenty minutes."
"They look busy."
"They're here to talk to us." She nudged him. "Ask one question. That's it."
He went to the smallest stall. "Excuse me, what do interns actually do at your firm?"
The architect laughed. "Mostly make models and coffee. Want to see?" She showed him photos, looked at his drawings, and gave him her card. "Email me in January."
Darshan walked back to Ritu, card clutched, legs shaking. "I have to write an email now."
"Yes. Tonight, while you're brave."

qa.q: Where was the career fair held?
qa.a: In the badminton hall.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling while standing by the stalls?
qa.a: He felt shy and nervous, too scared to walk up for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What made Ritu's advice useful?
qa.a: It broke the task into one question, which made it possible for Darshan to start a real conversation.

qa.q: How might the architect see Darshan's question?
qa.a: She seemed to find it honest and friendly, which is why she laughed, looked at his drawings and gave him her card.

grounding: Shows a young adult making a first professional contact at a career fair.

passage:
Dear Ms. Aditi Rao,
I heard you speak at our college on water management last week. I was the student in the third row who asked about village tanks.
I'm in my final year of civil engineering and have been reading about traditional rainwater systems. Your point that old designs still teach us something stayed with me.
I would be grateful for twenty minutes of your time to ask about your work. I am also looking for a summer internship, but I understand if that is not possible. Even a suggestion of what to read would help.
I have attached a short project I did on stepwells in my district.
Thank you for your time.
Warm regards,
Kiran

qa.q: What project did Kiran attach?
qa.a: A short project on stepwells in Kiran's district.

qa.q: How might Kiran have been feeling while writing this email?
qa.a: Kiran was probably nervous but hopeful, careful to be polite and not ask for too much.

qa.q: What makes this a good first networking email?

passage:
Okay, Vijay, you asked how I got the internship at the publishing house. Honestly, it started with a mistake.
I'm Bhavna. In second year I emailed ten companies a copy-pasted letter. Nobody replied. I felt invisible.
Then my professor said, "People help people they've met." So I went to every book launch in the city for three months. I stood at the back, nervous, holding a cold samosa. I asked one editor one question each time.
One of them, an older man who ran a small press, remembered me by the fourth launch. He said, "You again. What do you actually want?"
I told him. He gave me a two-week trial proofreading. I worked like mad.
That trial became a summer internship.

qa.q: How many companies did Bhavna email at first?
qa.a: Ten companies.

qa.q: How did Bhavna feel when nobody replied?
qa.a: Bhavna felt invisible and discouraged.

qa.q: What changed Bhavna's approach, and why did it work?
qa.a: The professor's advice to meet people; showing up in person again and again made the editor remember Bhavna.

qa.q: How might the editor have seen Bhavna by the fourth launch?
qa.a: He seemed curious and a little amused, noticing Bhavna's persistence and wanting to know what Bhavna really wanted.

grounding: A young adult describes building professional connections that led to an internship.

passage: I'm Karthik, Ojas's roommate. On Saturday he dragged me to the engineering alumni meet in the college auditorium. He'd printed ten copies of his CV and practised a two-line introduction in the mirror. For the first half hour he stood by the snacks table, holding his plate like a shield. Then he walked up to a woman from a water-treatment firm who'd given a talk and asked about a problem she'd mentioned, nothing about jobs. They talked for fifteen minutes. She gave him her card. That night he wrote her a short email thanking her and attaching his project on filters. On Wednesday she replied, offering a call about their summer internship. I don't know what he felt, but he read that email about six times.

qa.a: He printed ten copies.

qa.q: What does Ojas holding his plate like a shield suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt nervous and unsure about approaching strangers at first.

qa.q: How does Karthik see Ojas's evening?
